abstract: Neotame is an artificial sweetener that contains functional groups (carboxyl, amino) capable of chelating metal ions. Understanding the thermochemistry of its interactions with mono- and divalent metal cations helps elucidate how such molecules may participate in metal-ion mediated processes in biological environments. This task investigates the binding energetics of neotame with seven metal ions (Li⁺, Na⁺, K⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, Fe²⁺, Zn²⁺) by computing metal ion affinities (MIA) and Gibbs free energies (ΔG) for the gas-phase complexation reactions. The computed values provide intrinsic thermochemical data for ligand-metal interactions and reveal trends linked to ion size and charge.

abstract: In asymmetric catalytic reactions, the interaction between catalyst and substrate often involves multiple noncovalent contacts. Identifying which specific interaction determines the enantioselectivity is critical for rational catalyst design. One approach is to compute interaction energies between simplified catalyst fragments and probe molecules using symmetry-adapted perturbation theory (SAPT). If a particular type of interaction (e.g., a C–H···π contact) shows a strong linear relationship with experimentally measured enantioselectivities across a range of catalyst substituents, it can be regarded as a candidate enantiodetermining interaction. This task examines a series of substituted benzene catalyst fragments interacting with a benzene probe to test whether the total SAPT interaction energy for the C–H···π contact can explain the observed enantioselectivity trends.

abstract: In planar N=4 super Yang-Mills theory, on-shell diagrams elegantly encode scattering amplitudes and their leading singularities in terms of the Grassmannian Gr(k,n). For non-planar corrections, a systematic method to directly write the on-shell differential form of a reduced non-planar diagram as a rational function of Plücker coordinates (k×k minors) has been developed, bypassing the traditional boundary measurement. The main algorithm is combinatorial in nature: from the diagram's connectivity one constructs a set of matrices whose determinant ratios and associated Parke-Taylor denominators give the on-shell form. This task reproduces that method for a concrete non-planar MHV diagram.

abstract: Simulation of compressible two‑medium flows with immiscible interfaces often relies on the five‑equation transport model. This model couples the conservation of mass, momentum, and total energy with a non‑conservative transport equation for the volume fraction, using a stiffened equation of state to describe both gases and liquids. The challenge is to design a numerical method that (i) preserves uniform velocity and pressure at isolated material interfaces (Abgrall condition), (ii) maintains the volume fraction strictly between 0 and 1, and (iii) keeps partial densities and internal energy positive, even under extreme density and pressure ratios. This task centers on a quasi‑conservative discontinuous Galerkin (DG) spatial discretisation that satisfies the Abgrall condition, together with bound‑preserving and positivity‑preserving limiters tailored for the five‑equation model. The target is to verify these three properties through a set of one‑dimensional test cases: accuracy (order of convergence), equilibrium preservation, and robustness (bound‑preserving and positivity‑preserving behaviour).

abstract: Holographic complexity conjectures propose that the computational complexity of a boundary state is dual to certain bulk geometric quantities, such as the action (CA) or volume (CV) of specific spacetime regions. This task focuses on rotating BTZ black holes in three-dimensional anti-de Sitter space – a simple, tractable setting where angular momentum can be included. The goal is to understand how the presence of rotation influences the time dependence of complexity and the complexity of formation. In particular, the task investigates the full time profile of the CA complexity growth rate and the CA complexity variation with respect to the vacuum, as well as the dependence of the CV complexity of formation on angular momentum. The computed quantities will be checked numerically against reference implementations.

abstract: The mammalian brain contains hundreds of distinct cell types, each with specific molecular profiles and spatial distributions. Creating a comprehensive whole-brain atlas requires profiling millions of cells using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA‑seq) to define a transcriptomic taxonomy and then spatially resolving those cell types with multiplexed fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH). This task asks you to recompute the key computational pipeline that combines these two data modalities: you will build a hierarchical cell‑type taxonomy from public scRNA‑seq data and map a brain‑wide MERFISH dataset to that taxonomy, ending with the overall mapping accuracy and the final number of transcriptomic cell types found.

abstract: In confluent epithelial tissues, cells remain connected by cell–cell junctions as they move collectively. When two different cell populations meet—for example, normal (wild-type) cells and transformed (cancerous) cells—one population may invade the other. The outcome depends on the mechanical properties of each cell type and the adhesion energy between them. A key geometric parameter is the target shape index p⁰ = P⁰/√A⁰, which controls whether a cell type behaves as a solid-like tissue that resists neighbor exchanges or as a fluid-like tissue that readily rearranges. The vertex model predicts a critical shape index near 3.812 that separates these two regimes. Junction tensions between cells determine both the shape index and the cross-type adhesion, thereby controlling whether the two populations mix, segregate, or form isolated islands at the interface. This task reproduces the core simulation of an antagonistic migration assay: an underdamped active vertex model with two cell populations, testing three different junction-tension regimes.

abstract: Tumors contain a complex mixture of immune cells whose phenotypes influence cancer progression and response to immunotherapy. Understanding which cell states exist, how they differ between normal tissue and the tumor microenvironment, and whether they follow discrete categories or continuous activation trajectories is an open challenge. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) of CD45+ immune cells from breast carcinomas, matched normal breast tissue, blood, and lymph nodes provides a high-resolution view of the immune landscape. This task involves computationally processing such scRNA‑seq data to build an immune cell atlas, quantify how much phenotypic space expands in tumors compared with normal tissue, assess whether T cell activation follows a continuous gradient rather than discrete states, and examine the relationship between canonical macrophage activation signatures in the tumor microenvironment.

abstract: We consider the Rayleigh–Taylor instability (RTI) in which a heavy fluid is accelerated into a lighter fluid, causing the interface to become unstable and evolve into complex, vortical structures. The phenomenon arises in many applications, including astrophysics and inertial confinement fusion. Direct numerical simulation of the full compressible problem is expensive, so a multiscale model that decomposes the velocity into a compressible continuous part and an incompressible irrotational part has been proposed. The incompressible part controls the fine-scale Kelvin–Helmholtz roll-up of the interface and can be solved efficiently on a 1‑D parameterization, while the compressible part captures bulk dynamics on a coarse grid. This task implements that multiscale model and runs it on standard RTI test problems to produce key interface evolution quantities. Your job is to build the numerical solvers, execute the simulations, and output the required interface metrics — not to verify that the model agrees with any particular reference; that evaluation is done by the hidden scorer against independently known benchmarks.

abstract: Extracting infinite-volume three-particle scattering parameters from finite-volume lattice QCD energy levels requires solving the relativistic three-particle quantization condition. For identical scalar particles, this condition relates the finite-volume energy spectrum to the two- and three-particle K matrices via a determinant equation whose roots give the box energies. This task implements the quantization condition for identical scalar particles with s- and d-wave two-particle interactions, projects it onto cubic-group irreducible representations, and computes the resulting finite-volume spectrum for a given set of two-particle scattering parameters. The goal is to demonstrate a working numerical solver that can later be used to extract three-pion interaction parameters from lattice data.
